title: How should I structure my project to get the best no one shotting experience?
author: M1cahXD
selftext:
I’m starting a new game project and want to set things up properly from the beginning.

For those who have experience with larger or long term projects; what workflow would you recommend to avoid things becoming messy and difficult to maintain later on?


I'm using Godot, + agent 

I don't need it to create models and the map for me as I can do that myself. I'm looking for it to help build the actual systems.


Would love to hear what has worked well for you guys.

comments.author: Time_Cat_5212
comments.body: No expert here but I set up a repo with a bunch of protocols, routines, whatever and then iteratively produce a spec that breaks the project into phases with testable outcomes.  The repo structure is a container in which you can get a bunch of sessions working iteratively toward a bigger picture... Versus making something and then having to reinterpret it.

replies.author: M1cahXD
replies.body: That sounds awesome! Is it free or open source, that I could use my self?

replies.author: cowman3456
replies.body:
Git is open source.  There's a GitHub Desktop for windows which makes it a bit more approachable if you're unfamiliar.  

You should take time to learn git for version control... It won't take long.  Version control with a repository is fundamental to any project.  

Good luck!

comments.author: Ill-Past4609
comments.body: When I use codex I do /Plan describe my entire game, systems , core loop and end game you ask it to start with core loop and set it in phases.

replies.author: Beskull
replies.body:
I actually suggest using claude/openAi/perplexity to discuss your game and your outline. Then ask those engineers to give you a 'codex' prompt for your builder ... So it will build everything the way you want it to


Then test, iterate, and repeat

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
you have to define and communicate what is considered "quality" for AI. AI has no idea what you want outside of your prompts/instructions/documents. 

spend more time planning your project. write down every little detail. ask AI to organize these detail. Get some visual references etc (if you are using AI that can deal with visual references)

this may sound counterintuitive to you, but don't build demo/prototype for the project. Just build out the full projects in phases. (the additional context from the demo/prototype will confuse AI even if you spell it out later that "we are out of the demo phase". it will randomly pick up the bits and pieces as long as they are still part of the project folders. Asking AI to delete stuff is another can of worm)

lock down the folder structure also goes a long way. AIs are sensitive to naming conventions so naming your folders/files will go a long long way

comments.author: West_Satisfaction299
comments.body: Similar to what other people have said. When I first came up with the idea of my game. Codex told me itself not to one shot it and broke it down into lots of components. Took about 3 months to code all the components and combine them together.

comments.author: Beskull
comments.body:
Godot is untested for "long term" projects. I've built in Godot, unreal, and unity. Unity likely wins for a solid long term. 

That said, godot can work great if you are trying to get a limited scope game launched (indie size). I'm using it now, and losing boundaries for Godot. But if I was doing less experimentation, and wanted to set up a great foundation, I'd go unity. 

Unreal will make the best looking games (in general ... But you can do a run with shaders to make it look pretty good in other engines) 

For a stack: 
GitHub
Use Wave to put your cli's in... So you can have codex and/or Claude code and/or opencode.

Blender should be in your stack, but ai isn't great at creating shippable 3D morph targets and rigs. But it can create killer still models. 

Use fal.ai to source and create your temp art, sfx, and music. But I suggest finding artists for final game art and music. 

And if you use AI ... Use it to build yourself TOOLS. Not to build everything about the game. It will be too sloppy, and burn a ton of tokens if you just prompt your way through the game creation entirely. 


Hope that helps. Coming from my opinion.

comments.author: Officialpolygrafix
comments.body:
I gotcha.  
Game dev with 25 years experience and having worked on over 30 games at studios and indie.   
I run the ai process like a partnering coder and project manager/producer.  Got a pretty good system down. I'm 74 days deep and almost finished with a game that would have taken myself and a small team of about 3 others over a year to finish. It's a business management sim, with a full game economy and all the things your typical tycoon style game would have, (except mine is about managing a strip club).

Here's how i work:

* **Start with the tools.** Pick an AI coding assistant such as Claude, Codex, or Grok. Start with a lower-cost plan while you learn. Install Unity (i use unity because it has mcp tools. I don't know godot), then install and configure the third-party MCP for Unity package so your AI can interact with the editor. Ask the AI to walk you through setup.
* **Write the game design document before building.** Explain your idea to the AI and have it interview you about the features, gameplay, and gaps in your design. Spend real time going back and forth. You don’t need every answer yet, but you do need a solid starting point with room to grow.
* **Set up the project properly.** Have the AI create a local Git repository and a GitHub backup. Then ask it to turn your GDD into a development plan with prioritized milestones. Save the GDD and plan in the repo so future AI sessions can read them. Review the plan yourself before moving on.
* **Test the Unity connection.** Open Unity and connect MCP for Unity. Ask the AI’s chat side to write a small test prompt for its coding side. Run that prompt and confirm it can actually work with your Unity project.
* **Build one milestone at a time.** Have chat write a clear prompt for M1, then give it to a fresh coding session. Use a new coding thread for each milestone, labeled M1, M2, and so on. This keeps the work organized.
* **Playtest every milestone.** When the code is done, press Play in Unity. Keep a simple text file with notes under headings like “M1 playtest”: what works, what feels wrong, what broke, and any new ideas. Give those notes back to chat so it can adjust the plan and prepare M2.
* **Repeat.** Build, playtest, take notes, and refine. The AI can move quickly, but you’re still the one deciding whether the game is actually fun and working the way you imagined.

That’s my process in a nutshell. The initial setup and planning took me a few days, but it made everything afterward much easier to manage.

If you want to see what I’m making with it, feel free to follow along. Otherwise, good luck!

comments.author: Fresh_Sock8660
comments.body:
Treat it as a software development project.

The main problem you'll face is the ever growing line count on everything, but you can build tests for those. These are context length killers if left alone. 

Also do frequent reviews for god-classes and separation of concerns, but the above tests will solve most of it. 

Try not to ignore problems. For example, you see the agent often trying python3 but your environment only has python, either add a line to, e.g. agents.md with the python rule or create a symlink. 

I found that I'm the slowest part of the system so I invest substantially into building tools that make my participation as smooth as possible. For example, if we're testing between x visuals, then what I get to decide on is an image with the x labelled candidates. Scripts that launch at specific layers of the game or with the game setup to try a new mechanic without having to play the game to get to it.

So if you take anything from this, address your bottlenecks. The sooner the better.

comments.author: ipreuss
comments.body:
What I developed over time as guidelines for Claude:

\- in the plan phase, brainstorm at least three different architectural approaches for the new feature. Select the one (or a combination) that provides the best maintainability, even if it is more work.   
\- end the plan phase with an architecture reviewer that checks whether the plan creates a SOLID and DRY architecture, and a plan consistency reviewer, that checks whether the plan is consistent both internally and with what’s already there.   
\- when something is hard or “impossible” to test, create testability. Missing testability is never a reason to skip writing tests. Maintain and enhance an API that allows acceptance tests to play the game like a player would, and to access game state that allows testing for the results of player actions, including visuals.   
\- when implementation is finished, run the architecture reviewer again
